who_icf.title: International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF)
who_icf.application: Sole classification standard used to ground subgroup functional domains. WHO ICF supplies category codes and official category labels; the nine benchmark subgroup names, their combinations of codes and their relationship to task-construction needs are benchmark-defined operationalizations, not WHO-designated subgroups or clinical diagnoses.

design.user_group: Exactly one of visual, hearing, motor, cognitive; these are benchmark organizational groups, not a WHO ICF four-class taxonomy.
design.subgroup_ids: One or more broad, potentially overlapping ICF-informed functional/interaction support subgroups. The nine labels are defined by the benchmark; they are not official ICF categories, diagnostic classes, or prevalence strata.
design.need_ids: One or more IDs from the revised 14-entry documented_user_need_taxonomy.json, grounded in ISO/IEC 29138-1:2018.
design.relationship: need_id_to_subgroup_ids defines permissible candidate subgroups for each of the 14 Need IDs, not deterministic assignments. Annotators select only subgroups supported by the instantiated task and its user-facing accessibility requirement, independently of how the agent obtains information or performs actions.
design.assignment_policy: Assign one or more of the eligible subgroups only when relevant to the task realization. In particular, C3 notes/checklists need not be tagged time/prospective-memory, and C3 reminders need not be tagged short-term memory; similarly alternative-keyboard and input-timing requirements are distinct realizations under M2.
design.standard_basis: WHO ICF is the sole international classification basis for subgroup functional domains. The task-construction Need IDs are separately grounded in ISO/IEC 29138-1:2018. ICF-to-subgroup and Need-to-subgroup associations are benchmark-authored mappings, not official WHO or ISO crosswalks.
design.severity_and_diagnosis: No ICF severity qualifiers or clinically assessed disability statuses are assigned. Both V-S1 and V-S2 use b210 (seeing functions) because their non-visual versus low-vision task scenarios cannot be inferred as distinct diagnoses or severity grades from an ICF category code.
design.handoff: Subgroups characterize the user-facing access that tasks should enable at completion or takeover; the agent is not constrained to using the same modality or accessibility feature while completing the task.

V-S1.name: Blindness / non-visual access
V-S1.definition: Tasks requiring visual information or controls to remain accessible without reliance on vision, including user takeover through screen-reader, speech or other non-visual representations.
V-S1.standard_alignment: ICF b210 is the standardized seeing-functions domain. Non-visual access is the benchmark scenario, not a diagnostic classification derived from b210.

V-S2.name: Low vision / adaptable visual presentation
V-S2.definition: Tasks requiring individually usable visual presentation, including enlarged text or controls, contrast/colour adaptations, and perceivable alternatives for visually dense content.
V-S2.standard_alignment: ICF b210 is the standardized seeing-functions domain. The benchmark focuses on residual-vision presentation support; b210 itself does not distinguish this subgroup from V-S1 without clinical assessment.

H-S1.name: Deaf or hard of hearing / auditory access limitations
H-S1.definition: Tasks preserving alternatives to speech, sound and audio-only notifications, or an individually usable auditory presentation for later user interaction.
H-S1.standard_alignment: ICF b230 describes hearing functions, including auditory discrimination. The benchmark combines deafness and limited-hearing access scenarios under one operational subgroup.

M-S1.name: Keyboard input difficulty
M-S1.definition: Tasks supporting alternative text entry, serial key actions, adjusted key acceptance, or other alternatives to demanding physical-keyboard actions.
M-S1.standard_alignment: ICF d440 concerns fine hand use and b760 voluntary movement coordination. Keyboard access demands are benchmark instances of those broader domains, not named ICF subcategories.

M-S2.name: Pointer / fine-motor control difficulty
M-S2.definition: Tasks supporting alternatives to fine target acquisition, conventional pointing, dragging, continuous movement or precision mouse manipulation.
M-S2.standard_alignment: ICF d440, d445 and b760 cover fine hand use, hand/arm use and voluntary movement coordination. Pointer- and mouse-related tasks are benchmark operationalizations.

M-S3.name: Input control / timing difficulty
M-S3.definition: Tasks requiring keyboard or other input to accommodate unintended repetition, delayed responses, or strict input-timing constraints, for example adjustable repeat and acceptance settings.
M-S3.standard_alignment: ICF b760 anchors voluntary movement coordination. ICF b765 describes involuntary movement functions and is only contextually relevant when such movements are actually involved; input timing or accidental presses alone do not imply b765 impairment.

C-S1.name: Attention / comprehension and simplification support
C-S1.definition: Tasks reducing competing stimuli and unnecessary reading, language-processing or cognitive load to support focused, comprehensible interaction.
C-S1.standard_alignment: ICF b140 describes attention functions; b167 describes mental functions of language; d166 describes reading activity. The benchmark combines these as one interface-related support subgroup, not as a single WHO code.

C-S2.name: Memory / persistent-information support
C-S2.definition: Tasks supporting information retention and retrieval by keeping notes, checklists, bookmarks or other durable external representations available.
C-S2.standard_alignment: ICF b144 covers memory functions. Notes, checklists and persistent information artifacts are selected task-level supports rather than an ICF subgroup definition.

C-S3.name: Time / prospective-memory support
C-S3.definition: Tasks supporting future intentions, appointments and time-dependent actions through accessible reminders, calendars, alarms, timers or persistent time cues.
C-S3.standard_alignment: ICF b144 concerns memory, b164 higher-level cognitive functions including time management, and d230 carrying out daily routine. Calendar and reminder use operationalizes these domains, without claiming WHO defines prospective memory as a separate subgroup here.

subgroup_assignment_guidance.V3: Choose V-S1 for non-visual access to non-text material; V-S2 only when the task specifically supports residual visual perception or adapted visual display; assign both only when both are substantiated.
subgroup_assignment_guidance.M2: Choose M-S1 for sequential or adapted keyboard actions; M-S3 for time/acceptance/repeat or unintentional input control; assign both only for tasks that provide both kinds of support.
subgroup_assignment_guidance.M3: Choose M-S1 for keyboard-related alternative interaction; M-S2 for pointer/target-access alternatives; assign both only when both are supported.
subgroup_assignment_guidance.C3: Choose C-S2 for notes, checklists and durable recall cues; C-S3 for future-oriented reminders, calendars and time-management cues; assign both only for tasks explicitly addressing both.
subgroup_assignment_guidance.default: One eligible subgroup: select it when applicable to the scenario. Multiple candidates: choose based on the task-specific accessibility requirement; never automatically assign every candidate merely from Need ID.

migration.note: Subgroup functional classification is now grounded exclusively in WHO ICF. The 9 subgroup IDs and 14 Need ID candidates remain unchanged from the earlier ICF-informed JSON. Main text and JSON are now aligned on cognitive and motor mappings. Mapping task records and recomputing subgroup analyses still require task-level review.
